newsitem.title: CHINA: Two Koreas seen reaching accord in food aid talks.
newsitem.headline: Two Koreas seen reaching accord in food aid talks.

text.p: Officials of the Red Cross Societies of South Korea and its rival North were expected to reach agreement by Friday on the delivery of food aid to the hungry North, officials said.
However, several difficulties surrounding the actual delivery of the 50,000 tonnes of corn and other grains to North Korea were holding up the final accord, officials said on Thursday.

"We hope, if everything goes well, we can meet tomorrow at 10.00 a.m. (0200 GMT) to finalise our agreement," Lee Byoung-woong, secretary general of the South Korean Red Cross Society, told reporters at the end of a second day of talks in Beijing.
The two sides had reached agreement on sending a second batch of 50,000 tonnes of corn or corn equivalents to North Korea, but several issues remained to be discussed, he said.

The four main problems to be resolved concerned aid in the form of medical supplies and clothing, transparency of aid delivery, designation of recipient areas, and a visit by South Korean reporters to monitor the deliveries, he said.

"It's a delicate issue and not so easy to resolve," said John Schaar, regional delegation head for the International Federation of Red Cross (IFRC) and Red Crescent Societies, referring to the problem of designation.
Schaar, an observer, said the atmosphere of the talks had been relaxed and friendly even though contacts between Seoul and Pyongyang have long been coloured by deep mistrust.
"These people have got to know each other over three rounds of talks...so it's fairly painless now," said Schaar.
The basic framework for the second batch of 50,000 tonnes of food aid had long since been agreed, he added.
North Korea's Red Cross had on Wednesday initially asked for more aid for North Korea, which is on the brink of famine after floods destroyed much of its harvest in 1995 and 1996.

The South has voiced concern that previous food shipments may not have reached intended beneficiaries and had proposed future aid be sent via Panmunjom, the only border crossing between the two Koreas since the 1950-53 Korean War ended in an uneasy armistice.
North Korea refuses to use the land crossing at Panmunjom and has insisted that the aid be sent by sea.

Southern officials have said the latest package of food, similar to an amount agreed last May, would be available for delivery to the North by the end of October. The first shipment is due to be completed later this month.
They said the South was unable to meet the request from the North for a larger amount because the southern Red Cross had to rely on private donations.

International aid workers say the communist North is on the brink of famine after floods in 1995 and 1996 devastated much of the country's farmland and industrial bases, exacerbating already severe food shortages.
Pyongyang says severe drought is threatening to do even more damage to its agricultural sector this year.
The aid agreed on last May came on top of $16 million worth of donations made by Seoul in response to an appeal by the United Nations World Food Programme.
Washington also this month nearly doubled its total food aid to North Korea to $52 million, which is intended to combat widespread malnutrition, particularly among children.
